Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Genesis 11, drawn from the approved sources.

---

## Genesis 11 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### The Tower of Babel (vv. 1–9)

**Narrative Setting.** Genesis 11:1-9 explains *how* the scattering of nations described chronologically earlier in Genesis 10 actually came about. Moses places the Babel story after the Table of Nations as a "flashback" to show the cause of the dispersion. The unifying language was struck down by God, and the present multiplicity of languages stands as a monument to sin. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-11-commentary; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pride-of-babel-and-the-praise-of-christ)

**v. 1 — "Now the whole world had one language and a common form of speech."**
- Literally "one lip" and "one [set of] words" — both pronunciation and vocabulary were identical. This fits the biblical teaching of a common origin in Adam. The actual first language is unknown; the older view that it was Hebrew is now widely rejected. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-11-commentary; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/11.htm)
- Gill notes Jewish tradition held it was the "holy tongue" used at creation, but he observes that the eastern language family (embracing Hebrew, Syriac, Chaldee, and Arabic) was the original, though no single modern dialect preserves it purely. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-11.html)
- Ellicott notes that recent scholarship (for his day) tended to find a common basis between Sanskrit and Semitic tongues, and that primitive mankind had one language. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/11.htm)
- **Reformed/Calvin**: Calvin says community of language was a peculiar kindness of God to retain the sacred bond of society. The diversity of tongues is "repugnant to nature" and is a punishment divinely inflicted. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html)

**v. 2 — "And as people journeyed eastward, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there."**
- "Journeyed" literally refers to pulling up tent-pegs — the human family as a band of nomads. "From the east" is better rendered "eastward" (as in Genesis 13:11). Shinar is the region of ancient Babylon/Babylonia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/11.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/11.htm)
- The people were refusing to obey God's command to "fill the earth" (Genesis 9:1). Instead of spreading out, they clustered. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-11-commentary; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pride-of-babel-and-the-praise-of-christ)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes)**: There was a general population shift from the mountains of Armenia (where the ark landed) to the plains of Shinar, where topography and climate made life easier. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-11.html)

**v. 3 — "Come, let us make bricks and bake them thoroughly." So they used brick instead of stone, and tar instead of mortar."**
- The alluvial plain of Babylon lacked stone but had rich clay deposits. Kiln-fired bricks were far more durable than sun-dried ones. "Tar" (bitumen/asphalt) was plentiful in that region, bubbling up from subterranean deposits. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-11.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-11.html)
- Guzik notes a theological link: baked brick and asphalt were the same materials Noah used to waterproof the ark (Genesis 6:14) and Moses' mother used for the basket (Exodus 2:3). The builders were building a waterproof tower, revealing their distrust of God's promise never to flood the earth again. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)
- **Reformed/Calvin**: The difficulty of the work — making bricks without stone and using bitumen for mortar — aggravates their guilt. They were not deterred by hardship because they rushed impetuously against God like madmen. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html)
- **Precept Austin (Ross article)**: The Hebrew cognate-accusative construction for brickmaking (nilbənâ ləbēnîm) has a striking parallel in the Akkadian *Enuma Elish* (libittasu iltabnū), where bricks were molded for a year before the tower was raised. This is one of several literary connections between Genesis 11 and Mesopotamian building accounts. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-11-commentary)

**v. 4 — "Come," they said, "let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of all the earth.""**
- The sin was twofold: (1) the love of praise — "make a name for ourselves"; (2) the love of security — building a city to avoid being scattered, in defiance of God's command (Genesis 9:1). The city and tower were outward expressions of these inward sins. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pride-of-babel-and-the-praise-of-christ)
- Guzik argues the tower was likely an observation point for astrological/occult practices, not a literal attempt to reach heaven. If they wanted to reach heaven, they would have started on a mountain, not a sea-level plain. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes)**: The tower was likely a temple dedicated to the "powers" or signs of heaven represented by the zodiac — a monument to man's ingenuity and religious rebellion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-11.html)
- Gill rejects the common view that the tower was a flood-protection refuge. The plain between the Tigris and Euphrates was the worst place for that. The real aim was fame and the perpetuation of their name. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-11.html)
- **Reformed/Calvin**: Calvin is emphatic — the flood-refuge theory has no basis in the text. The sole motives were "mad ambitions and proud contempt of God." They sought an immortal name on earth, which is perpetual infatuation: to neglect heaven and seek immortality where everything is fading. "As soon as mortals, forgetful of themselves, are inflated above measure, it is certain that like the giants, they wage war with God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html)
- **Reformed (Ligonier)**: Calvin writes that humanity gathered not to worship but "to excite war against God." The pattern of Babel — city, autonomy ("Let us…"), cohesion, making a name — is deliberately contrasted in the very next chapter with Abram: tent, God's sovereignty ("I will…"), separation, given a name, altar of worship. An entire theology of self-justification by human effort versus divine justification through faith is apparent. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/tower-babel)
- **Precept Austin (Ross article)**: The major sin was not building a city or tower per se, but the attempt of the whole human race to live in *one* city — striving for unity, security, and social immortality in defiance of God's desire for them to fill the earth. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-11-commentary)

**v. 5 — "Then the LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of men were building."**
- This is anthropomorphic language — God is omniscient and omnipresent. The "descent" is a figure to show how feeble man's attempt really was: the tower that was supposed to reach into God's abode was so tiny that He had to "come down" to evaluate it. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/tower-babel)
- **Reformed/Calvin**: God "for a little while seemed to take no notice of them," bearing with the wicked so that when He suddenly breaks off their work, His judgment is more decisive. "The Lord therefore descended that he might see; that is, he evidently showed that he was not ignorant of the attempt." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html)
- Guzik sees the personal character of the language as suggesting a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ (a Christophany). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)
- "Sons of men" (bene ha adam) — Gill and others note this phrase may distinguish the irreligious builders from the "sons of God" (the faithful line of Shem), implying Noah, Shem, and the godly remnant were not involved in the project. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-11.html)

**v. 6 — "And the LORD said, 'If they have begun to do this as one people speaking the same language, then nothing they devise will be beyond them.'"**
- God is not threatened; He is describing the dangerous potential of unified, fallen humanity. When sinful people unite in rebellion, the potential for evil is enormous. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pride-of-babel-and-the-praise-of-christ)
- **Reformed/Calvin**: Calvin detects a "suppressed irony" — God ironically smiles at their foolish confidence, as if to say, "This people is compacted in a firm conspiracy; by what method can they be broken?" Yet He will blow upon them and scatter them without difficulty. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html)
- **Baptist (Piper/Desiring God)**: God's statement does not imply divine impotency but recognizes the dangers of collective apostasy. Depraved men eagerly join together to fight against God and His people. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pride-of-babel-and-the-praise-of-christ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/tower-babel)

**v. 7 — "Come, let Us go down and confuse their language, so that they will not understand one another's speech."**
- "Let Us" — the plural is widely seen as a reference to the Trinity (cf. Genesis 1:26). Calvin rejects the Jewish view that God addresses angels, arguing God places those to whom He speaks "in the same rank with himself." The passage is "not improperly adduced in proof that Three Persons subsist in One Essence of Deity." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)
- "Go to" (or "Come") is an ironical echo of the builders' own "Go to" (or "Come") in vv. 3-4. What man proposes in pride, God answers in judgment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/11.htm)
- The confusion did not mean every individual spoke a different language (which would make society impossible), but that families/nations each received their own tongue. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/11.htm)

**v. 8 — "So the LORD scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they stopped building the city."**
- The scattering was both judgment and mercy. It forced compliance with God's original command to fill the earth, and by dividing humanity linguistically and geographically, God slowed the collective rebellion of fallen mankind — preventing even greater evil. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-11-commentary)
- **Reformed/Calvin**: This was not the honorable dispersion of God's original blessing but a "violent rout" — the principal bond of union between them was cut asunder. Men who had been distributed with honor were now "ignominiously scattered, driven hither and thither like the members of a lacerated body." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html)
- **Baptist (Piper/Desiring God)**: "The languages of the world are the judgment of God on sin, and they are designed by God for the global glory of Jesus Christ." God has built into the world a system by which the pride of different groups restrains the pride of other groups. Thousands of languages limit the global aspirations of arrogant mankind. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pride-of-babel-and-the-praise-of-christ)
- The text does not rule out the possibility that those who remained in the area (later Babylonians) eventually finished the city or tower. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/11.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-11.html)

**v. 9 — "That is why it is called Babel, for there the LORD confused the language of the whole world…"**
- The Hebrew name *Babel* is derived from *balal*, "to confuse" or "to mingle." This is a deliberate Hebrew wordplay. The popular Babylonian etymology ("Gate of God") is thus refuted by Scripture: Babel represents not a gate to heaven but divine confusion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/undoing-of-babel)
- **Reformed/Calvin**: "Behold what they gained by their foolish ambition to acquire a name!" They hoped for an everlasting memorial; instead God branded them with eternal disgrace. They gained a name, but not the one they wanted. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html)
- **Precept Austin (Ross)**: Later prophets, especially Zephaniah 3:9–11, appear to construct an antithesis to Babel: pure speech (one language), gathering of the dispersed, removal of pride, and service on the holy mountain. Pentecost (Acts 2) is often seen as a harbinger of that reversal — where tongues were confused at Babel, at Pentecost the Spirit enabled understanding across all tongues. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-11-commentary)
- **Reformed (Ligonier)**: Babel represents man's unified futile attempt to reach up to heaven, but it became a fissure through which judgment came down and confused language into "babbling." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/undoing-of-babel)

**Catholic view (from search excerpt)**: The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the descendants of Noah migrated from Armenia southward along the Tigris, then westward into the plain of Shinar. As their numbers grew, they said, "Come, let us make a city and a tower, the top whereof may reach to heaven; and let us make our name famous before we be scattered abroad into all lands." God confounded their tongue. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15005b.htm)

### Genealogy: Shem to Abram (vv. 10–26)

**v. 10 — "This is the account of Shem. Two years after the flood, when Shem was 100 years old, he became the father of Arphaxad."**
- This genealogy traces the Messianic line from Shem through to Abram (Abraham). It is the line followed in Luke 3:23-38. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)
- **Reformed/Calvin**: God reckons the years of the world from Shem's line as a mark of honor — not due to the family's merits, but because of God's gratuitous adoption. Yet Calvin notes that a great part of Shem's posterity apostatized. God chose Arphaxad alone from Shem's many sons, then Salah alone, then Eber alone, until Abram — "the calling of whom ought to be accounted the renovation of the Church." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes)**: This genealogy traces the "godly line" through which the promised Redeemer would come. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-11.html)

**v. 12 — "When Arphaxad was 35 years old, he became the father of Shelah."**
- The BSB text follows the Hebrew Masoretic text. Some ancient versions (LXX) insert Cainan between Arphaxad and Shelah (cf. Luke 3:35-36). This is a well-known textual variant but not addressed in detail by the consulted sources for this verse.

**vv. 10–25 — The Declining Lifespans.**
- **Precept Austin (Bridgeway)**: The genealogy shows the human lifespan was shortening dramatically after the flood, as God had announced (Genesis 6:3). Shem lived 600 years; by the time of Nahor (v. 25), the total lifespan was down to 148 years. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/genesis-11.html)
- **Precept Austin (Bridgeway)**: The genealogy from Eber onwards traces the line through Peleg (Eber's elder son, producing Abram), whereas the genealogy in Genesis 10 traced through Joktan (Eber's younger son, producing Arab tribes). The ten names listed may be ten leading men of the period rather than a complete father-to-son chain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/genesis-11.html)

**v. 16 — "When Eber was 34 years old, he became the father of Peleg."**
- The name Peleg means "division," and Genesis 10:25 notes that "in his days the earth was divided." This likely refers to the Babel dispersion. Calvin calculates that the confusion of tongues occurred around the time of Peleg's birth (about 101 years after the flood). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html)

**v. 24 — "When Nahor was 29 years old, he became the father of Terah."**
- Nahor and Terah were the grandfather and father of Abraham. The promise of the Deliverer from the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15) would find its fulfillment through this family. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)

---

### The Family of Terah and the Call of Abram (vv. 27–32)

**v. 26 — "When Terah was 70 years old, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran."**
- This is the first mention of Abram in Scripture. Abram (later Abraham) is mentioned 312 times in 272 verses. Genesis spends almost a third of its text on his life. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)
- Abram is not listed first because he was the firstborn, but because of his prominence in the narrative. Terah was 70 when he *began* having sons; Abram may have been born when Terah was 130 (since Terah died at 205 and Abram was 75 when he left Haran, per Genesis 12:4). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)

**v. 27 — "This is the account of Terah. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. And Haran became the father of Lot."**
- Lot, Haran's son, will become a significant figure in the patriarchal narratives (Genesis 13, 14, 19). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)

**v. 28 — "During his father Terah's lifetime, Haran died in his native land, in Ur of the Chaldeans."**
- Haran died before his father — an unusual and tragic turn noted in the text. Ur of the Chaldeans was a major city in southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), known archaeologically as a centre of moon-god worship. Joshua 24:2 confirms that Terah's family served "other gods" there. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)

**v. 29 — "And Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. Abram's wife was named Sarai, and Nahor's wife was named Milcah…"**
- Milcah was the daughter of Haran (Abram's deceased brother), making her Nahor's niece. Iscah, also mentioned, is sometimes identified by Jewish tradition with Sarai herself, though the text does not explicitly say this. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)
- Nahor's marriage to Milcah produced Bethuel, who later became the father of Rebekah (Genesis 24). The family lines remain intertwined. Guzik notes Sarai's name may mean "contentious." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)

**v. 30 — "But Sarai was barren; she had no children."**
- This note is theologically crucial. Sarai's barrenness sets up the great miracle of Isaac's birth and the testing of Abram's faith. Because Abram's name means "exalted father," his childlessness must have been an awkward embarrassment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)

**v. 31 — "And Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot… and they set out from Ur of the Chaldeans for the land of Canaan. But when they arrived in Haran, they settled there."**
- Acts 7:2-4 clarifies that God's call to Abram (Genesis 12:1-3) came while he was *still in Ur*, before the move to Haran. Abram's obedience was only partial in at least two ways: (1) he brought his father Terah and nephew Lot, though God said "from your family"; (2) he stopped in Haran instead of continuing to Canaan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)
- **Baptist (Spurgeon, cited by Guzik)**: Spurgeon is quoted: "Half-way obedience increases our responsibility, because it is a plain confession that we know the Lord's will, though we do it not. Abram had received the call, and knew that he had done so, else why had he come to Haran? He admitted, by going as far as Haran, that he ought to go the whole way to Canaan; and so, by his own action he left himself without excuse." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)

**v. 32 — "Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran."**
- Terah's death in Haran freed Abram to move on — Genesis 12 begins immediately after this. The name *Terah* likely means "delay," and *Haran* means "parched, barren." When Abram was in partial obedience, delay and barrenness marked his life. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)
- Spurgeon (cited by Guzik): "The result of this to Abram was the absence of privilege. God spoke not to his servant in Haran: neither dream, nor vision, nor voice came to him in the place of hesitancy. The Lord loved him, but hid his face from him, and denied him the visits of his grace." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)

## Distinctive Protestant Traditions on Key Points

**Reformed/Presbyterian (Calvin, Ligonier)**:
- The Babel narrative is a prime example of total depravity: even after the flood, humanity's first collective act was rebellion. Calvin stresses God's sovereignty: the tower was so puny God had to "come down" to see it. The scattering was both punishment and a restraining grace. Babel contrasts with Abram: self-justification versus justification by faith. Babel's ziggurat was man reaching up; the gospel is God coming down. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-11.html; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/tower-babel; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/undoing-of-babel)

**Baptist (Piper/Desiring God, Spurgeon, Garner-Howes)**:
- Piper emphasizes that the scattering produced peoples and languages that, while a judgment on sin, were simultaneously *designed by God for the global glory of Christ*. God builds into the world a system of competing prides that restrain each other. The ultimate reversal comes at Pentecost and will be consummated when every tribe and tongue worships Christ. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pride-of-babel-and-the-praise-of-christ)
- Spurgeon (via Guzik) stresses the personal application of Abram's half-obedience: delay and barrenness are the spiritual consequences. Garner-Howes focuses on the tower as astrological/idolatrous worship. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-11.html)

**Charismatic/Pentecostal (Guzik/Enduring Word)**:
- Guzik sees the "Let Us go down" of v. 7 as a Trinitarian reference, and the Lord's descent in v. 5 as a possible pre-incarnate Christophany. The waterproof tower reveals the builders' secret disbelief in God's flood promise — they trusted their own engineering over God's word. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-11/)

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (via Precept Austin / Allen P. Ross article)**:
- Ross argues the predominant idea is not the tower itself but the *scattering*. The sin was not building a city but attempting to have the entire race live in one city. The passage is not a Hebrew adaptation of the Greek Titans myth. The narrative shares significant literary parallels with the Akkadian *Enuma Elish* (brickmaking ritual, raising the tower's head to heaven, the cognate-accusative construction for brickmaking), suggesting the Genesis account is a deliberate theological polemic against Babylonian pride — but set centuries earlier than Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-11-commentary)

**Catholic**:
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes the same basic reading: migration from Armenia south and west, building with brick and bitumen, divine confusion of tongues as punishment for pride. No distinctively Catholic doctrinal interpretation emerged from the consulted pages beyond the shared traditional reading. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15005b.htm)

**Orthodox and other views**: No material was found from the specified Orthodox sources (oca.org) or from prosperity/Word of Faith/Hyper-grace teachers in the searches conducted.
